title: Friends above all
hookLine: Epicurus: of all wisdom provides for a happy life, the greatest is friendship (Principal Doctrines 27)

cards: Before you choose a restaurant, do you think about the food, or about who's coming? Epicurus had a firm answer.

Seneca, the Stoic, passes it on in one of his letters: look first for whom you'll eat and drink with, before you look at what you'll eat and drink. Eating without a friend, he says, is the life of a lion or a wolf.
Strong words from a man known for simple food.

teach.b: First, the doctrine. Epicurus left a set of short sayings, the Principal Doctrines. Number twenty-seven says, in plain words: of all the things wisdom provides for a happy life, by far the greatest is friendship.
Second, why a philosopher of pleasure ranks it first. A friendship may begin from need, Epicurus said: someone helps you, you help them. But it becomes worth having for its own sake.
And it carries something else: confidence.

Another of his sayings puts it this way: it isn't so much our friends' help that helps us, as our trust that they'd help if we needed it. That trust takes a great deal of fear out of life. Third, how the Garden lived it.
Diogenes Laërtius says Epicurus had so many friends that whole cities couldn't count them.

In his will, which Diogenes preserves, Epicurus provided for his birthday to be kept every year, for his students to meet together every month, and for the children of his friend Metrodorus, who had died.
The Stoics also prized friendship, but they called it a good only between people of virtue, and wanted the wise person to be able to stand alone if friends were lost.

Epicurus wanted friendship close to the center of the good life. Two schools, both serious about friends, weighting them differently. And to Epicurus, a good meal with no one across the table was hardly a meal at all.

how: Epicureans, ancient and modern, place friendship at the center of a good life, sharing meals, keeping in touch and caring for one another's families.

games.q: you're planning dinner. by Epicurus's advice, what do you decide first?
games.why: Epicurus, through Seneca: look first for whom you'll eat and drink with. eating without a friend is the life of a lion or a wolf.

practice: Let a few friends come to mind, one at a time, no ranking, and settle on one you trust, someone who would help if you needed it. Epicurus said that trust does more for us than the help itself.
Stay with their face a moment, then ask when you last made real time for them, not a quick message, but time.
